message.content:
**How to kill Visual Studio Code (`code.exe`) with `taskkill`**

| What you want to do | Command | Notes |
|---------------------|---------|-------|
| **Kill all instances of `code.exe` immediately** | `taskkill /IM code.exe /F` | `/IM` matches the image name (process name). `/F` forces termination. This will close every `code.exe` that is running – useful when you have several windows open. |
| **Kill a specific instance by its Process ID (PID)** | `taskkill /PID <pid> /F` | First find the PID with `tasklist | findstr code.exe`. Replace `<pid>` with the number you got. |
| **Kill all child processes of a given `code.exe`** | `taskkill /IM code.exe /F /T` | `/T` terminates the specified process and any child processes it spawned. VS Code’s renderer processes are usually children, so this helps clean up everything. |
| **Filter by window title (e.g., only kill “Visual Studio Code” windows)** | `taskkill /IM code.exe /F /FI "WINDOWTITLE eq *Visual Studio Code*"` | Useful if you have other unrelated `code.exe` processes (unlikely, but safe). |

### Quick one‑liner

```cmd
taskkill /IM code.exe /F
```

This will close every VS Code window you have open.

---

#### Why `taskkill` works

- **`/IM`** – matches the executable name (`code.exe`).  
- **`/F`** – forces the process to terminate (no graceful shutdown).  
- **`/T`** – optional flag to also kill child processes.  

If you prefer a more graceful shutdown, you can omit `/F` and let VS Code exit normally. However, if the editor is frozen or unresponsive, `/F` is the quickest way to get rid of it.

---

#### Using PowerShell instead (optional)

If you’re on PowerShell, you can achieve the same with:

```powershell
Stop-Process -Name code -Force
```

or, to target a specific PID:

```powershell
Stop-Process -Id <pid> -Force
```

But since you asked about `taskkill`, the CMD commands above are what you’ll need.
